extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of The Spectator; playwrights, authors, and social observers
extracted.subtask_description: Essayistic guidance and social critique on how to produce comic effect, compose stage-plays, and portray characters and social behaviour; also commentary on coffee-house society and ethnographic judgement. Useful for playwrights, essayists, and social commentators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of wit that produces laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man of wit makes us laugh, it is by betraying some oddness or infirmity in his own character, or in the representation he makes of others; when we laugh at a brute or inanimate thing, it is at some action or incident that bears a remote analogy to any blunder or absurdity in reasonable creatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter arises from perceived absurdity or a blunder mirrored in human behaviour; comic effect should come from exposing oddness or infirmity rather than mere shock. Use analogy to human error to make non-human incidents funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required of a conversational 'Butt'
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is not qualified for a 'Butt' who has not a good deal of wit and vivacity, even in the ridiculous side of his character; a stupid 'Butt' is only fit for ordinary people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective conversational 'Butts' must give play to men of wit by active, lively absurdity; an accomplished butt can turn ridicule back upon his attackers. Example: Sir John Falstaff as an ideal 'Butt'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose whether to speak or listen in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you fall into a man's conversation, first consider whether he has a greater inclination to hear you or that you should hear him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilful flatterers often speak little and practise attentive listening. Assess interlocutors' appetite to speak; when in doubt, be an engaged listener rather than forcing speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of good company / 'worthier part of mankind'
rubrics_metrics.description: The persons most worthy of regard are those not too active or too warm in spirit: men whose entertainments are derived from reason rather than imagination, showing no impatience or instability in speech or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters (and social companions) formed for society should be temperate, steady, and reasonable—good fathers, generous brothers, sincere friends, and faithful subjects. Aim to depict such temperate characters in essays and plays to model civic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model public-spirited man (Eubulus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who enjoys fortune without launching into expense, exerts useful qualities without public employment, dislikes overt thanks, lends money at legal value for the good of friends, and uses his authority peacefully in local society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray civic virtues through discreet beneficence and wisdom: influence that leads others to better behaviour, avoiding ostentation and seeking public advantage rather than private praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on lascivious or 'luscious' expressions on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Luscious (lascivious) expressions are commonly used by authors when they lack wit; writers, who want to please but cannot otherwise, help out with a little smuttiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bawdy material is often a sign of poverty of invention. Playwrights should avoid using sexual or bawdy content as a crutch to elicit applause; instead, cultivate genuine wit and thoughtful plotting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use actors/actresses merely as titillation to cover weak writing
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet flags in writing, a pretty girl or lascivious gesture can supply the audience's appetite; dull poets use such devices like parasites use their patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on actors' physical charms or gratuitous stripping/exposure to make up for weak dialogue or absent invention; such devices degrade the moral tone and alienate modest audience members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic moral design: punish vice rather than reward it
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet turned his comedy so that the rake or seducer were found out at the catastrophe and met with contempt accordingly, the audience could be diverted and instructed at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure plays so that vice is reproved and virtue rewarded; using moral consequences rather than flattering or rewarding immoral behaviour will both entertain and benefit the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal character construction: combine virtue and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: A man that is temperate, generous, valiant, chaste, faithful and honest may, at the same time, have wit, humour, mirth, good-breeding, and gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who embody noble virtues together with wit and sociability; such characters can instruct and delight, showing that true taste and enjoyment flow from sound morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors resort to bawdry when lacking genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers who want to raise laughs but lack genius commonly keep in reserve 'luscious' expressions, double meanings, and lascivious gestures to create claps and laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise these anti-patterns as evidence of weak invention; critics and editors should be wary of works that substitute smut for wit and seek to encourage more imaginative solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of ethnocentric judgement of foreign customs
rubrics_metrics.description: We are all guilty in some measure of the same narrow way of thinking, fancying the customs, dress, and manners of other countries are ridiculous and extravagant if they do not resemble our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing or judging other cultures (in travel writing, satire, or dramatic portraits), avoid simple ridicule; seek to understand practices in their context and use foreign perspective to reflect on one's own society.
